papers.what_it_is: Proposes quantum circuit learning (QCL), a hybrid scheme that trains a low-depth parameterized circuit by classical gradient updates, with function-approximation arguments and small numerical simulations.

assertions.value: Mitarai et al. argue that a QCL circuit can approximate any analytical function given enough qubits, using a single-qubit-rotation input encoding whose tensor-product structure supplies high-order polynomial terms; nonlocal entangling operations are what expose the nonlinearity. This is a constructive in-principle argument, not a formal theorem with a resource bound.
quotes: We theoretically show that a quantum circuit driven by the QCL framework can approximate any analytical function
Entangling nonlocal operations are the key ingredients of the nonlinearity of an output.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as an in-principle argument for a simple input encoding; the paper itself says at least in principle.

assertions.value: For gates generated by a Pauli product, the exact gradient of an observable expectation with respect to a circuit parameter can be evaluated on the quantum circuit by measuring expectation values with the gate shifted by plus and minus pi/2 (parameter-shift rule).
quotes: While we cannot evaluate the commutator directly, the following property of commutator for an arbitrary operator ρ enables us to compute the gradient on a quantum circuit:
assertions.certainty_reason: The identity is derived analytically in the paper for gates of the form exp(-i theta P/2).

assertions.value: In classical simulation (with added sampling-style noise) of a 6-qubit, depth-6 circuit, QCL fits x^2, e^x and sin x well and fits |x| less well, and also performs a simple nonlinear 2-class classification; these are simulation results only, not hardware runs.
quotes: All of the functions are well approximated by a quantum circuit driven by presented QCL framework.
In this simulation, we allow output to be multiplied by a constant a which is initialized to unity.
assertions.certainty_reason: Small numerical simulations at N=6 qubits with a single fixed Hamiltonian, as the paper states.

assertions.value: The authors suggest QCL may offer a quantum advantage because it uses an exponential number of basis functions directly, but state that the learning cost and the problems where such an advantage holds still need investigation; no advantage is demonstrated.
quotes: This is a possible quantum advantage of our framework, which was not obvious from the previous approaches like QVE or QAOA.
Further investigations are needed including the learning costs and which actual learning problem enjoys such an advantage.
assertions.certainty_reason: Explicitly framed as a possible advantage with open questions.

papers.partial_detail: 106-page review (arXiv v1, Sept 2017). Read abstract, contents, Introduction, the Section VI opening and executive summaries of every subsection of VI and VII, the quantum PAC learning and qRAM/amplitude-encoding remarks in VI, and the Outlook in full. Classical background (II) and sections IV, V, VII bodies only skimmed via executive summaries. Predates quantum-inspired classical dequantization results.
papers.what_it_is: Broad review of machine learning and artificial intelligence in the quantum domain, covering quantum speed-ups for learning, quantum generalizations of learning concepts, and quantum learning agents.

assertions.value: Most quantum linear-algebra-based ML speed-ups in the review assume pre-loaded quantum databases (qRAM) and efficient preparation of amplitude-encoded states. qRAM access to classical data does not by itself imply that amplitude-encoded states can be generated efficiently.
assertions.anchor: Sec. VI.C remark before amplitude-encoding algorithms; Outlook
quotes: assumes universal quantum computers, and often data prepared and accessible in quantum database
does a-priori not imply that quantum amplitude encoded states can also be
assertions.certainty_reason: A reviewer's statement about assumptions in cited work, not a proof.

assertions.value: As of the review (2017), work on quantum-enhanced ML and AI was mostly theoretical and conceptual, with hardly any dedicated experiments showing how quantum mechanics can be exploited for ML.
quotes: Most of the work in this new area of research is still largely theoretical and conceptual, and there are, for example, hardly any dedicated experiments demonstrating how quantum mechanics can be exploited for ML and AI.
assertions.certainty_reason: Time-stamped survey judgement (2017); likely outdated for hardware experiments since.

assertions.value: In the review's account, uniform-distribution k-juntas can be learned by a quantum algorithm whose gain lies in classical processing time rather than query complexity; these separations depend on access to coherent quantum example oracles.
quotes: have shown that there exists a quantum algorithm for learning k-juntas using
Note the improvement in this case is not in query complexity, but rather in the classical processing
assertions.certainty_reason: Cited results from other papers (Atici-Servedio), summarized by the reviewers.

assertions.value: The review concludes that for most quantum-ML topics both the achievable edge over the best classical solutions and the practical implementability remain widely open questions.
quotes: a) what are the limits/how much of an edge over best classical solutions can be achieved, and b) could the proposals be implemented in practice in any reasonable term.
For most of the topics discussed, both questions above remain widely open.
assertions.certainty_reason: Reviewers' stated assessment as of 2017.

papers.what_it_is: Proposes a quantum feed-forward neural network built from general quantum perceptrons, with a fidelity-based training algorithm that needs qudits only for adjacent layers, benchmarked in classical simulation on learning an unknown unitary.

assertions.value: The proposed quantum neural networks can carry out universal quantum computation; a construction in the appendix shows this even for commuting 4-level qudit perceptrons within each layer.
quotes: It is a direct consequence of the quantum-circuit structure of our QNNs that they can carry out universal quantum computation.
a QNN comprised of quantum perceptrons acting on 4-level qudits that commute within each layer, is still capable of carrying out universal quantum computation
assertions.certainty_reason: Constructive argument in Appendix C reducing to universal two-qubit gates.

assertions.value: The training algorithm computes parameter matrices layer by layer, so the qubit/memory requirement scales with network width rather than depth; the price is that many repeated network evaluations are needed to estimate the cost-function derivative.
assertions.anchor: Main text, training algorithm and discussion
quotes: we need only access two layers at any given time, which greatly reduces the memory requirements of the algorithm.
This remarkable reduction does come at a price, namely, we require multiple evaluations of the network to estimate the derivative of the cost function.
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows from the algorithm design; the repeated-evaluation cost is stated by the authors but not quantified.

assertions.value: In classical simulations with 2 and 3 qubit input spaces learning a random unitary, the trained QNN matched a theoretical estimate of the best achievable test cost from few training pairs and was robust to corrupted training pairs. Only very small widths could be simulated.
quotes: the QNN matches the theoretical estimate and demonstrates the remarkable ability of our QNNs to generalise.
As illustrated in Fig 3b the QNN is extraordinarily robust to this kind of error.
assertions.certainty_reason: Pilot simulations at m=2 and 3 qubits only; authors acknowledge exponential simulation cost.

assertions.value: The authors report not observing barren plateaus when training their QNNs from random initialization, in small simulations; they give only an intuitive explanation (fresh ancillas per layer) and no proof.
quotes: We always initialised our QNNs with random unitaries and we did not observe any exponential reduction in the value of the parameter matrices K
assertions.certainty_reason: Observation from simulations of a handful of qubits; no scaling analysis.

papers.what_it_is: Presents quantum algorithms for cluster assignment and k-means-style cluster finding that claim time logarithmic in the number and dimension of vectors, assuming qRAM-stored data.

assertions.value: Under the assumption that data are stored in quantum random access memory, the paper claims supervised cluster assignment takes time O(log(MN)) on a quantum computer versus O(poly(MN)) for the best known classical algorithm.
quotes: takes time O(log(M N )) on a quantum computer, compared with time O(poly(M N )) for the best known classical algorithm.
when the data is stored in a quantum random access memory (qRAM), this mapping takes
assertions.certainty_reason: Complexity claim from algorithm analysis conditional on qRAM; the classical comparison is to the best known algorithms, not a proven lower bound.

assertions.value: The paper claims an exponential speed-up for evaluating distances and inner products of post-processed vectors versus classical sampling, citing Aaronson for the apparent classical hardness, and says quantum ML can be logarithmic in both vector count and dimension.
quotes: Quantum machine learning can take time logarithmic in both the number of vectors and their dimension, an exponential speed-up over classical algorithms.
assertions.certainty_reason: Speed-up is stated against known classical algorithms and relies on qRAM state preparation.

assertions.value: Optimal k-means is NP-complete and not expected to be solved in polynomial time classically or quantumly; the adiabatic seed-finding and clustering routine can only be expected to give approximate solutions, and its average-case performance is left open.
quotes: Indeed, optimal kmeans is an NP-complete problem which we do not expect to solve in polynomial time on a computer, classical or quantum.
The question of how well the adiabatic algorithm performs on average is an open one.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limitation themselves; the minimum-gap scaling is not analyzed.

papers.partial_detail: Read the abstract, introduction, framework, all five theorem statements, numerical results, discussion and the proof-sketch part of Methods in full; appendix proofs (Appendices B-E, about 3,600 lines) were not read line by line.
papers.what_it_is: Proves generalization-error bounds for variational quantum machine learning models in terms of the number of trainable gates, with numerics on QCNN phase recognition and unitary compiling.

assertions.value: For a quantum machine learning model with T trainable local gates trained on N points, the generalization error is bounded, with high probability, at worst on the order of sqrt(T log T / N); hence polynomially many trainable gates need only polynomially many training points.
assertions.anchor: Abstract, Theorem 1, Remark 1 (proof in Appendix C)
quotes: We show that the generalization error of a quantum machine learning model with T trainable gates scales at worst as
Theorem 1 (Basic QMLM). For a QMLM with T parameterized local quantum channels, with high probability over training data of size N , we have that
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as a theorem with proof in the appendix; applies to arbitrary data distributions and loss-bounded models.

assertions.value: If only K of the T gates change substantially during training, the bound improves to one scaling at worst linearly with K and logarithmically in the total number of parameterized gates M T.
quotes: then the generalization error will scale at worst linearly with K and logarithmically in the total number of parameterized gates M T
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 3 is a special case of the stated mother theorem with appendix proof; the bound depends on optimizer-dependent change measures.

assertions.value: In classical simulation, QCNN phase classification generalized from few training points, and QFT compiling needed training data linear in qubit number for random computational basis inputs and constant (up to 9 qubits) for Haar-random inputs, which the authors say is consistent with their bounds.
quotes: Our numerical investigation shows a linear scaling of the training requirements when training on random computational basis states.
Up to n = 9 qubits, we generalize well from a constant number of training data points, independent of the system size.
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical simulations at modest sizes; the near-solution initialization result (N=2) assumes prior knowledge of the solution.

assertions.value: The bounds do not prove a quantum advantage, and they give no non-trivial guarantee for models with exponentially many independently trainable gates, where the bound itself scales exponentially in the number of qubits.
quotes: Our results do not prove a quantum advantage of quantum over classical machine learning.
our generalization error bounds scale exponentially with n, and hence we do not make non-trivial claims about this regime.
assertions.certainty_reason: Explicit limitation stated by the authors.

papers.partial_detail: 43-page review. Read abstract, introduction, Section 2 opening (2.1) and section headings, Section 3 opening, 3.4 Quantum Machine Learning, 3.6 final remarks, and Sections 4 and 5 in full; application subsections 3.1-3.3, 3.5 and technical subsections 2.2-2.11 were not read in detail.
papers.what_it_is: Literature review of quantum annealing as a heuristic optimization method, its D-Wave hardware and software stack, and industrial application studies including quantum machine learning.

assertions.value: As of the review (arXiv v3, June 2022), the authors know of no industrial application where quantum annealing unquestionably outperforms classical heuristic algorithms, and whether QA can give a quantum speed-up is still debated.
quotes: to the best of our knowledge, there is no industrial application where QA unquestionably outperforms classical heuristic algorithms.
While the question of whether QA can provide a quantum speed-up over classical approaches is still subject of a scientific debate
assertions.certainty_reason: Survey-level judgement, dated to 2022 and scoped to the authors' knowledge.

assertions.value: The mapping of dense logical QUBO graphs onto the sparse connectivity of current QPUs is identified as probably the most crucial common bottleneck of quantum annealing for real-world applications.
quotes: The mapping from these dense logical graphs to the sparse connectivity in QPUs prevents efficient computation in the current generation quantum annealers.
This is probably the most crucial and common bottleneck of QA for real-world applications.
assertions.certainty_reason: Reviewer synthesis of many application studies on D-Wave-generation hardware.

assertions.value: Quantum annealing as implemented drops the guarantees of the adiabatic theorem; the authors regard it for practical purposes as a stochastic black-box combinatorial optimizer similar to simulated thermal annealing.
quotes: Although inspired by Adiabatic Quantum Computation, QA is implemented with more relaxed conditions, thus removing the theoretical guarantees of the adiabatic theorem
For all practical purposes, QA is therefore a stochastic black-box optimization approach for combinatorial optimization, similar to simulated thermal annealing.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' stated characterization; conclusive evidence for quantum benefit is described as elusive.

assertions.value: In the review's survey of quantum-annealing machine learning (classification, clustering, matrix factorization, reinforcement learning), no clear advantage over classical machine learning has been demonstrated, and deep densely connected ML models are poorly matched to sparse annealer topology.
quotes: So far, no clear advantage of QA-based approaches over classical machine learning could be demonstrated, but some aspects are promising.
For ML, it is standard to have many layers of densely connected variables, something that is directly orthogonal to the regular sparse topology of current quantum devices.
assertions.certainty_reason: Review-level judgement as of 2022 across small-scale studies.

papers.what_it_is: Introduces warm-starting QAOA and recursive QAOA from solutions of continuous relaxations (QP or SDP with Goemans-Williamson rounding), with portfolio and MAXCUT simulations.

assertions.value: Initializing QAOA from a Goemans-Williamson rounded cut, with the modified mixer and nonzero regularization, lets the circuit represent the GW cut, so the quantum algorithm can retain the classical GW approximation ratio at any depth p.
quotes: In particular, this allows the quantum algorithm to inherit the performance guarantees of the classical algorithm.
Therefore, WS-QAOA is at least as good as GW rounding.
assertions.certainty_reason: Short argument that the variational form can recover the GW cut; assumes optimization reaches at least the initial-state energy.

assertions.value: In classical simulations of 6-asset portfolio problems (250 instances at depth 1) and MAXCUT instances, warm-start QAOA and recursive QAOA gave better solutions than standard versions at low depth; these are small simulations without hardware noise.
quotes: Our simulations show that warm-starting quantum heuristics provides an advantage at low depth.
assertions.certainty_reason: Small simulated instances (n=6 for portfolio, up to 30 nodes for MAXCUT), advantage measured against standard QAOA, not best classical solvers.

assertions.value: Under the Unique Games Conjecture it is impossible for quantum or classical polynomial-time algorithms to improve on the Goemans-Williamson guarantee for MAXCUT unless NP-hard problems can be solved in polynomial time; improvement is possible only if the conjecture is false.
quotes: Under the Unique Games Conjecture [83, 84], it is strictly impossible to improve upon the guarantees of GW using either quantum or classical algorithms
assertions.certainty_reason: Conditional on the unproven Unique Games Conjecture, which the paper states is neither proven nor disproven.

assertions.value: With the GW-based warm start and the modified mixer, the initial state is no longer a mixer eigenstate, so the standard adiabatic-theorem argument for convergence to the optimum as depth grows no longer applies; convergence is only studied numerically.
quotes: Since the prepared initial state is no longer an eigenstate of the mixer (otherwise we would not be able to deviate from it) we cannot use the same arguments as in [16] to derive the convergence of the
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limitation explicitly and defer to numerics.
